text: Grammar Girl here. I'm Inyan Fugarty. This week we'll talk about how tiny writing mistakes
label: content

text: in ballot measures have changed what the law appears to say. And then we'll look at where
label: content

text: the phrase batten down the hatches comes from.
label: content

text: But before we get started, I have a newsletter that I almost never tell you about, but that
label: content

text: you'd probably enjoy. Every week I send out a short writing tip, links to both the episodes
label: content

text: that week, and a link to something completely unrelated that I happen to enjoy. You can
label: content

text: subscribe by going to quickanddirtytips.com. And then in the upper right, there's an icon that
label: advertisement

label: advertisement

text: And we'll put that link in the show notes too. It's election day in the United States, which means
label: content

text: we've all been reading a lot of voter guides, or at least I hope you have. Be informed people.
label: content

text: So today we're going to look at why good writing matters a lot in these often boring documents.
label: content

text: Let's start with a decimal point. In 2006, Arizona voters considered Proposition 203,
label: content

text: which was supposed to fund early childhood programs by increasing the cigarette tax.
label: content

text: The backers meant to raise the tax by 80 cents per pack. But the ballot's explanation of
label: content

text: what a yes vote would do described it as an increase of 0.80 cents per pack. And those
label: content

text: aren't the same thing. If you write 80 cents, you mean 80 pennies. You can also write that
label: content

text: amount with a dollar sign as $0.8, but 0.8 cents means 8 tenths of one cent, so the
label: content

text: ballot's version was actually a hundred times smaller than the intended tax. The word decimal
label: content

text: itself is all about ten. It comes from the Latin de chimus, meaning tenth, and the phrase
label: content

text: decimal point has been used in English since at least 1711. In the Arizona summary, that
label: content

text: tiny decimal point before the 80 made a huge difference. In fact, the Arizona Republic
label: content

text: reported that the difference could lead to about $186 million in lost revenue. And despite
label: content

text: its significance, the error survived drafting, review by the Attorney General's Office, printing,
label: content

text: 40 public meetings. Finally, a sharp-eyed newspaper reader noticed the problem, but unfortunately
label: content

text: after early voting had started. Fortunately, though, the full text of the initiative was
label: content

text: more clear. It specified a tax of four cents for each cigarette, which worked out to 80
label: content

text: cents for a standard pack of 20. After voters approved the measure, Arizona's Attorney
label: transition

text: General decided the state could actually collect the full intended 80 cents because the law
label: content

text: was written correctly. It was just the summary that was wrong.
label: content

text: Now, moving on to another Arizona initiative, we have another math-related problem. In 2018,
label: content

text: supporters of an education funding initiative circulated petitions showing that their proposal
label: content

text: would raise certain income tax rates by quote, 3.46% and by 4.46%.
label: content

text: But the proposed law said it would add 3.46 and 4.46 percentage points to the existing rates.
label: content

text: Compared with the original rates, those changes actually represented huge increases.
label: content

text: If you were talking percentages, the taxes would have gone up approximately 76% and 98%.
label: content

text: A percentage increase tells you the size of a change relative to the original number.
label: content

text: A percentage point increase tells you the numerical difference between two percentages.
label: content

text: For example, if a tax goes from 5% to 10%, it's gone up by 5 percentage points.
label: content

text: points. But it has also gone up by 100% because the new rate is twice as much as the old
label: content

text: rate. In this Arizona case, the Supreme Court said the petition description was misleading
label: content

text: and removed the entire initiative from the ballot, even though supporters had already
label: content

text: collected about 270,000 signatures. One inaccurate use of the word percent helped sink the whole
label: content

text: effort. Although to be fair, that wasn't the only problem, but it did come into play.
label: content

text: Next, we leave Arizona and move to Oregon. In 1996, Oregon voters approved property tax
label: content

text: measure 47. But according to an article from the Oregon State Bar, the measure was so hard to interpret
label: content

text: that Oregon's deputy attorney general later said much of state government became paralyzed
label: content

text: because nobody could determine exactly what the measure meant.
label: content

text: Oregon lawmakers drafted a replacement in 1997,
label: content

text: Measure 50, that made things more clear.
label: content

text: But because Measure 47 had amended the state constitution,
label: content

text: they couldn't just handle the problem themselves.
label: content

text: Voters had to vote on it again, making it an expensive edit.
label: content

text: Finally, we have a purely grammatical example.
label: content

text: When California voters approved Proposition 47 in 2014,
label: content

text: one of its sentences discussed resentencing under a list of laws, and then continued.
label: content

text: It was supposed to say something like,
label: content

text: this section provides that resentencing is to take place, pursuant to sections blah blah blah,
label: content

text: as those sections have been amended or added by this act.
label: content

text: But the final proposition left out the word as.
label: content

text: So instead, it read, this section provides that resentencing is to take place,
label: content

text: pursuant to sections blah blah blah, comma, those sections have been amended or added
label: content

text: by this act.
label: content

text: So now it ran two ideas together.
label: content

text: An appellate judge later pointed out that without the word as, the second part became
label: content

text: an independent clause, violating the rules of punctuation and creating a comma splice,
label: content

text: and he thought this essentially stripped the remaining part of any logical purpose.
label: content

text: In fact, he pointed to the missing as an example of an obvious drafting error that a court
label: content

text: could correct.
label: content

text: But he also said judges have to use, quote, great restraint, unquote, when they're thinking
label: content

text: about correcting voter-approved language so that fixing a mistake doesn't end up rewriting
label: content

text: a law to say something the voters didn't actually want.
label: content

text: So there you go, a decimal point made a tobacco tax a hundred times smaller.
label: content

text: Confusing percent with percentage points helped knock a whole initiative off the ballot.
label: content

text: An incomprehensible Oregon measure had to be fixed and voted on again, and a missing
label: content

text: AZZ created a comma splice in California's criminal code that a judge later highlighted
label: content

text: as an obvious drafting error.
label: content

text: Proofreading ballot initiatives is a high stakes activity that takes more than just checking
label: content

text: spelling and punctuation.
label: content

text: You have to check the numbers, the units, the definitions, the summary, and more.
label: content

text: So the next time someone tells you tiny writing details don't matter, you can point them
label: content

text: to the decimal point that put $186 million in tax revenue at risk.

text: Next, I've been trying to prepare my house for the big storms
label: content

text: we're supposed to get this winter in California.
label: content

text: So the phrase, batten down the hatches, has been on my mind.
label: content

text: This next segment is by Samantha Enslin.
label: transition

text: Has anyone ever told you to batten down the hatches?
label: content

text: Well, if so, they were telling you to prepare for trouble.
label: content

text: Maybe they saw your boss walking angrily down the hall,
label: content

text: or maybe they heard the principal call you to his office.
label: content

text: Well, either way, they were warning you
label: content

text: that a metaphorical big storm was coming
label: content

text: and that you'd better get ready.
label: content

text: Batten down the hatches is what sailors used to say
label: content

text: when a real storm was coming.
label: content

text: You see, all ships have hatches or hatchways.
label: content

text: These are square or rectangular holes in the deck,
label: content

text: and you can use them to load cargo
label: content

text: into a ship's interior or hold.
label: content

text: You can also climb down through the hatches
label: content

text: to get to the living quarters below deck.
label: content

text: In old sailing ships,
label: content

text: hatches were covered with an open wooden grating
label: content

text: that prevented sailors from falling through the hatches
label: content

text: as they walked across the deck.
label: content

text: That's kind of important.
label: content

text: And they also let fresh air and sunlight flow down
label: content

text: to the lower decks of the ship.
label: content

text: But these open gratings were not so great during storms.
label: content

text: If water crashed over the bow of the ship
label: content

text: and ran across the deck,
label: content

text: you wouldn't want it to flow down into the hatches.
label: content

text: Your ship would fill with water
label: content

text: and could even potentially sink.
label: content

text: So to solve this problem,
label: content

text: you can batten down the hatches.
label: content

text: Here's how.
label: content

text: One, grab the grating and place it in the hatch.
label: content

text: Two, then take a big piece of canvas tarpaulin
label: content

text: and lay it over the hatch.
label: content

text: Three, now get four battens,
label: content

text: long, thin strips of wood like yardsticks.
label: content

text: The word batten comes from a Middle English word
label: content

text: to describe a finished board
label: content

text: and it's related to the word baton.
label: content

text: Four and finally, nail those battens into each side
label: content

text: of the hatch, securing the canvas tightly across the top.
label: content

text: Congratulations, you have just made the hatch watertight.
label: content

text: In other words, you've battened down the hatches.
label: content

text: So that's your little tidbit for today.
label: content

text: Battened down the hatches is a nautical term
label: content

text: that now also metaphorically means to prepare for trouble.
label: content
